title: Black Friday-proof your email with a backup provider
summary: Your busiest sales week is the worst time for an email outage. Set up Bird as your backup provider in October, and switch in minutes when it counts.
body_markdown:
Black Friday is the one weekend your email can't take a day off. Order confirmations, shipping updates, and the doorbuster promotion you spent a month on all go out in the same few days. If your email provider has an outage or starts throttling your sends in the middle of that, each hour of delay shows up in your revenue and in your support queue.


The fix is a plan B: a second email provider that is already set up, verified, and sending real mail, so switching on the day takes minutes. This post walks through setting up Bird as that plan B, with a deadline for each step, and the first deadlines fall in early October.


## Why "we'll switch if it happens" doesn't work


Opening an account with a second provider takes a few minutes. Getting it ready for peak volume takes weeks, and most of that time is spent waiting on things you can't speed up:


- **DNS takes time.** A new record can take from a few minutes to 24–48 hours to reach DNS resolvers, depending on your DNS host and TTL settings. That's a long time to wait in the middle of Cyber Monday.
- **New accounts start small.** Peak volume needs a paid plan with sending limits sized for your busiest hour, set up and funded before you need it.
- **Mailbox providers are wary of strangers.** Gmail and Outlook judge mail by its sending history, and a sudden spike from a source they haven't seen can be throttled or filtered.
- **Your lists live at the old provider.** The addresses that bounced, complained, or unsubscribed are stored with the provider you're trying to get away from.


Each of these is easy to finish in October, which keeps it off your plate in peak week.


## Step 1: Publish your DNS records early


DNS is the step to start with: it's quick for whoever manages your domain, and it's the slowest to fix in a hurry. Bird's records sit right next to your current provider's, so nothing about today's sending changes:


Record What it does Effect on your current provider


DKIM (TXT) Proves Bird may send for your domain None. Bird uses its own selector, so your current DKIM record stays untouched.


Return path (CNAME) Handles bounces and covers SPF for mail sent through Bird None. It lives on a subdomain such as` send.yourdomain.com` , so your main SPF record stays as it is.


DMARC (TXT) Tells mailbox providers what to do with unauthenticated mail None. Your existing DMARC record already counts.


Link tracking (CNAME) Gives open and click tracking a branded hostname None. It's optional, but if you report on opens and clicks, publish it and turn tracking on for the domain.


Skip the inbound MX record (it would move your incoming mail to Bird), and if your current provider already uses` send` for its return path, give Bird's another name, such as` bounce` .


Bird checks the records automatically, and most domains verify within minutes of DNS propagation. Once verified, leave the records where they are: Bird re-checks them daily, and if the DKIM, return-path, or DMARC record keeps failing for 24 hours, sending from that domain pauses. A January DNS clean-up that deletes records nobody recognizes can quietly switch off your plan B, so tell your DNS owner why they're there.


[Sending domains](https://bird.com/docs/guides/email/sending-domains) has the full setup, and there are walkthroughs for[Cloudflare](https://bird.com/docs/knowledge-base/dns-and-domains/cloudflare) ,[Route 53](https://bird.com/docs/knowledge-base/dns-and-domains/route-53) , and[other DNS hosts](https://bird.com/docs/knowledge-base/dns-and-domains/generic-registrar) .


**Deadline:** six weeks before your peak.


## Step 2: Decide how you'll switch, and practice it


A backup helps when someone knows when and how to use it. Get your team to agree on four things before November:


- **The mechanics.** If your app sends over SMTP, switching is a credentials change: point it at Bird's[SMTP relay](https://bird.com/docs/guides/email/smtp) and use an API key as the password. Give promotional mail its own key set to the marketing category, so unsubscribes are honored. If it calls your current provider's API, have engineering build the Bird integration now and put it behind a switch they can flip without a release.
- **The trigger.** Write down what makes you switch, such as an incident on your provider's status page, a jump in deferred or bounced mail, or sends stuck in a queue. Then name the person who makes the call (and a deputy for when they're asleep).
- **The order.** Order confirmations, password resets, and shipping updates move first, because those are the emails customers chase. Promotions sent from your app follow once the switch is confirmed.
- **The edge cases.** A provider that times out may still have sent the message, so decide whether timed-out messages are resent and accept the odd duplicate.


Then rehearse. Bird's[mail sandbox](https://bird.com/docs/guides/email/testing-sandbox) runs test sends through the real pipeline to special addresses that simulate a delivery, a bounce, or a suppressed recipient, so your team can practice the switch without a single email reaching a customer.


**Deadline:** build the switch four weeks before your peak, and rehearse it two weeks before.


## Step 3: Bring your suppressions with you


Emailing people who already bounced, complained, or unsubscribed damages your sender reputation, so import those lists before the backup sends a single real email. Bounces and complaints become suppressions that block all mail to the address, and unsubscribes become marketing opt-outs that still let receipts and password resets through.


You can add up to 1,000 addresses at a time under **Email** > **Suppressions** , and engineering can import longer lists through the API. Our[migration guides](https://bird.com/docs/guides/email/migrate) cover eleven providers, with where to export each list and how their event names map to Bird's (handy for keeping your reporting intact if you switch). In the week before peak, import whatever was added since your first export, so October's unsubscribes are covered too.


**Deadline:** four weeks before your peak, with a top-up one week before.


## Step 4: Warm up the backup before you need it


Give the backup real work well before peak. Pick one steady transactional stream, such as password resets or shipping updates, and send it through Bird from four weeks out. You'll prove the setup works with real recipients, and mailbox providers will have seen your mail through Bird long before the volume arrives.


While you're at it:


- **Check your capacity.** Paid Email plans have no monthly volume cap, and higher tiers raise your sending speed, so pick the tier whose limits cover your peak sending rate on the[Email pricing page](https://bird.com/pricing/email) . Email is charged from your wallet as you send, so top it up before peak week.
- **Order dedicated IPs early, if you want them.** Bird warms a new dedicated IP automatically over roughly 30 days, and anything the IP can't take yet flows through the shared pool, so your mail keeps going at full volume. Buying an IP doesn't move your traffic by itself, so make the dedicated pool your default once warm-up finishes. Dedicated IPs are available on the Growth 250 and Scale plans.
- **See where your mail lands.** Two weeks out, run a seed test in[Inbox Insights](https://bird.com/docs/guides/email/inbox-insights) to check inbox placement at each mailbox provider.


**Deadline:** order dedicated IPs six weeks before your peak, and start the steady stream four weeks before.


## Your peak-season calendar


Count back from your peak date. Here's the calendar for Black Friday 2027 (Friday, November 26), with Cyber Monday on November 29. For Singles' Day, Boxing Day, or a big launch, shift the whole table to your own date.


When Black Friday 2027 What to have done Why then


8 weeks before Fri, Oct 1 Pick your plan, decide on dedicated IPs, and name one owner for the backup. Gives the later steps room to breathe.


6 weeks before Fri, Oct 15 Publish and verify your DNS records, order dedicated IPs, and fund your wallet. DNS can take up to 48 hours, an unverified domain is removed after about 14 days, and IP warm-up takes about 30 days.


4 weeks before Fri, Oct 29 Import suppressions and unsubscribes, map your events, build and sandbox-test the switch, then start the steady stream. Gives the backup a few weeks of real sending history.


2 weeks before Fri, Nov 12 Rehearse the switch end to end, run a seed test, and write down the trigger. Leaves time to fix whatever the rehearsal turns up.


1 week before Fri, Nov 19 Top up suppressions, freeze DNS changes on your sending domains, check plan limits and wallet balance, and confirm who's on call. A required record that fails for 24 hours pauses sending.


Peak week Nov 22–29 Watch your primary provider, and switch transactional mail first if the trigger fires. This is the week the preparation is for.


After peak December onward Keep the records published and the steady stream running. Your plan B stays ready for December and next year.


## Why Bird makes a good plan B


Bird is built to slot in next to the provider you already use. Our DKIM selector, return-path subdomain, and tracking hostname are new names, so publishing them changes nothing about how you send today, and your existing DMARC record already counts. If your app speaks SMTP, switching is a matter of new credentials. Dedicated IPs warm up on their own with overflow to the shared pool, and paid Email plans put no cap on monthly volume.


Standing by doesn't waste money either. A paid plan's monthly payment lands in your wallet as balance, and unused balance carries forward (nothing expires at renewal), so what builds up during a quiet month is still there on Black Friday.


[Get Started](https://bird.com/dashboard/signup) and have your plan B verified this week, or[Contact Sales](https://bird.com/demo?product=email) to talk through peak volumes, sending limits, and dedicated IPs.
